bibliographic.title: Reproducibility: The New Frontier in AI Governance
bibliographic.venue: Workshop on Technical AI Governance (TAIG) at ICML 2025, Vancouver, Canada
bibliographic.citation_apa: Mason-Williams, I., & Mason-Williams, G. (2025). Reproducibility: The new frontier in AI governance. Workshop on Technical AI Governance (TAIG) at ICML 2025, Vancouver, Canada.

methodology.method_family: policy commentary drawing on replication crises in other scientific domains
methodology.study_design: conceptual commentary with cross-domain comparative lens
methodology.technology_context: AI research broadly, with secondary mention of LLM capability evaluations and deep learning research practices

eligibility.decision_rationale: The paper argues that weak reproducibility protocols erode policymakers' ability to enact meaningful AI governance and recommends preregistration, increased statistical power, and negative-result publication. Provided text contains no discussion of conversational systems, chatbots, agents, RAG, guardrails, observability, audit logs, human oversight of deployed conversational AI, or sector-specific regulated deployment of LLM conversational systems. It is relevant as foundational context on meta-level AI governance and scientific standards for risk assessment, but not as central evidence for conversational governance in regulated LLM environments.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Extracted metadata conflicts with PDF front matter on year and venue; confirm bibliographic fields and whether workshop paper status affects inclusion.

appraisal.notes: Conceptual commentary without empirical sample; objective and recommendations are clearly stated, but limitations of the commentary approach are not explicitly discussed in the provided excerpts. Replication code link is provided.

cerqual.explanation: The argument is internally coherent and clearly links reproducibility standards to policymaker capacity for AI governance, but the provided text offers no direct evidence on conversational AI governance, operational controls, or regulated deployment contexts central to the review scope.

coding.theme: Reproducibility as a governance mechanism for AI policymaking
coding.subtheme: Scientific standards to improve trustworthy evidence for AI risk prioritization

synthesis.main_claim: Weak reproducibility in fast-moving AI research lowers the signal-to-noise ratio available to policymakers, undermining effective AI governance, and stronger reproducibility protocols should be treated as core governance tools.
synthesis.contribution: Frames reproducibility—via preregistration, larger-sample statistical power, and publication of negative results—as a policy-relevant governance intervention, illustrated through analogies to replication crises in other scientific domains.
synthesis.limitations: Provided text does not address conversational AI systems, operational deployment governance, or regulated-sector implementation; limitations of the commentary itself are not clearly stated in the excerpts.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as foundational/contextual evidence on how scientific reproducibility standards can support AI governance and policymaker decision-making; do not use as central evidence for conversational governance, human oversight of LLM interactions, or operational compliance controls.

evidence.claim: Paper focuses on AI governance for policymakers via reproducibility standards.

evidence.claim: Weak reproducibility erodes policymaker capacity to govern AI.
